verdicts.text: The `.getOutput("...")` method is a valid Pulumi API for retrieving named outputs from a `StackReference` or Terraform state reference object.
verdicts.evidence: Half of this claim holds. `StackReference.getOutput(name: Input<string>): Output<any>` exists in the Node SDK ("Fetches the value of the named stack output"). The current pulumi-terraform SDK is different: its state functions (getRemoteReference, getLocalReference, getS3Reference, getAzureRMReference) return a result with only `readonly outputs: {[key: string]: any}` and no `getOutput` method. So `.getOutput("...")` on a Terraform state reference would fail; you need `.outputs["..."]` or `.apply(r => r.outputs[...])` instead.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The older pulumi-terraform v5 `RemoteStateReference` class had `getOutput`, so the doc may be written against that older, now-replaced API. I couldn't read the reviewed file at that path to see which API its examples actually use.

Every language example in the guide uses FileAsset (or fn::fileAsset / fileasset) for index.html.
verdicts.framing_note: The link target and its #assets anchor both resolve, and the concept page describes FileAsset uploading a file as a storage bucket object's body, which is what the guide describes.

verdicts.text: You must use methods supplied in the Pulumi SDK to access an output's value once it is known.
verdicts.evidence: The Node.js SDK source doesn't let you read an Output's value directly. Calling toString raises OutputToStringError: "Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported. To get the value of an Output<T> as an Output<string> consider either: 1: o.apply(...) 2: pulumi.interpolate ...". That backs the claim that you need SDK methods such as apply/all/interpolate to get at the value.
verdicts.framing_note: Checked against the Node.js SDK only; the other language SDKs work the same way (apply/all), but this session didn't fetch their source.

verdicts.text: Users can register their organization's templates in the Pulumi Cloud New Project Wizard for convenient access.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's docs and launch blog describe this feature: "Pulumi Cloud now supports registering your own custom templates for your organization which will be made available in the New Project Wizard." Organization templates require the Enterprise or Business Critical plan, and the claim doesn't say so.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim doesn't mention that organization templates are limited to the Enterprise and Business Critical editions, so a plain "Users can register" may overstate who has access.

verdicts.text: Once an ESC environment is set up and projecting pulumi configuration, that environment (or multiple environments) can be imported into a Pulumi stack.
verdicts.evidence: The claim (config.md L775) links to three pages, and all of them exist in the repo and back it up. The outputs page has a `## pulumiConfig` section ("values that should be exported as stack configuration for Pulumi IaC"). The pulumi-iac guide says "The `environment` block in your stack configuration file (`Pulumi.<stack>.yaml`) lists the environments the stack imports" and shows an example that imports more than one environment.
verdicts.framing_note: The linked guide describes importing one or more environments through the stack's `environment:` block, which is what the claim says.

verdicts.text: The gke-secrets-encryption policy requires GKE clusters to have Application-layer Secrets Encryption enabled.
verdicts.evidence: The generated page's data file lists policy "gke-secrets-encryption" with description "Require GKE clusters to have Application-layer Secrets Encryption enabled". The claim is an accurate transcription of that entry (the remediation sets databaseEncryption.state: "ENCRYPTED").
verdicts.framing_note: The reviewed .md path doesn't exist locally; checked against the source data file for the generated page instead.

verdicts.text: The 'application-gateway-tls' policy requires Application Gateway to have secure TLS configuration.
verdicts.evidence: I checked the page's source data file. The policy named "application-gateway-tls" has the description "Require Application Gateway to have secure TLS configuration", so the doc text matches its data.
verdicts.framing_note: The page is generated from data, so this is a transcription claim checked against the policy metadata.

verdicts.text: Secrets have the same type, Output<T>, as unencrypted resource outputs, differing only in being marked internally as needing encryption before persisting in the state file.
verdicts.evidence: In the Node.js SDK, secrets are the same Output class (OutputImpl<T>). The only difference is an internal `isSecret` flag: "Whether or not this output wraps a secret value. Values which are marked as secret are stored in an encrypted format when they are persisted as part of a state file."
verdicts.framing_note: "differing only" is slightly loose: the same flag also carries secrecy through all/apply to derived outputs and masks the value in CLI display. Both effects come from the same internal marker.

verdicts.text: Go is one of the supported languages for this Pulumi AWS get-started tutorial.
verdicts.evidence: This line describes how the tutorial itself is built. Line 30 of the page offers `{{< chooser language "typescript,python,go,csharp,java,yaml,hcl" / >}}`, and lines 46-51 are the `choosable language "go"` block listing the Go prerequisites. Go is a standard Pulumi language, and nothing here is a checkable claim about a third party.

verdicts.text: This Pulumi program (as shown in the chosen language example) creates an NGINX deployment and exports the name of the deployment.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) This sentence only summarizes the page's own example programs. It makes no independent claim about the product. The examples do create an nginx Deployment and export its name in every language (e.g. TS L290 `export const name = deployment.metadata.name;`, YAML L519-520 `outputs: name: ${deployment.metadata.name}`), so the description matches the page.

verdicts.text: In every Pulumi language, an unhandled error raised inside an `apply` callback is reported as a deployment failure, causing `pulumi up` to abort the update and print the error in its diagnostics.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't check this against product source because the GitHub code search hit a rate limit (HTTP 403). The reviewed page (L631) itself hedges the claim with "(with one Go-specific exception described below)". Its Go note (L685) says an error returned from an `ApplyT` whose output is thrown away "is silently dropped and the update succeeds". So the unqualified "in every Pulumi language" doesn't match the page's own Go caveat.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/apply.md L631, L685; gh search code pulumi/pulumi (rate-limited)
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Every Pulumi language" is at odds with the page's own Go exception: in Go, errors from unused ApplyT outputs are reportedly swallowed. The author should qualify the opening sentence, or the Go behavior should be checked in sdk/go.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference says `pulumi package publish` will "Publish a package to the Private Registry. ... The package can be a provider or a schema." It also says "When <provider> is specified as a local path, Pulumi executes the provider binary to extract its package schema." So publishing an executable-based (binary provider) package to the Private Registry is supported.
